headline: How Owning Power Plants Became Digi Power X's AI Moat
lede: As lead times for large power transformers stretch toward four years, the limiting factor in America's AI data center build-out has turned out to be not silicon but steel and copper. Digi Power X (DGXX), a Miami-based AI infrastructure operator, argues that its ownership of existing power plants — with electrical substations already in place — lets it bypass the equipment queue that is stalling competitors. Investors on X have amplified this as a story about a specific Siemens procurement win, though the details remain unverified in public filings.
body:
The transformer shortage is real and severe. Demand for large power transformers has risen 119% since 2019; demand for *generator step-up* units — which raise a power plant's output to transmission voltage — is up 274%. Average lead times hit 128 weeks by mid-2025, with specialized units taking three years from order to delivery. Prices have risen roughly 80% in five years. By one industry estimate, more than half of planned U.S. data center projects for 2026 are projected to be delayed or cancelled for want of transformers, switchgear, or other power hardware. With Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META), and Microsoft (MSFT) collectively projecting north of $650 billion in AI capital expenditure, the bottleneck is no longer compute — it is the unglamorous copper-wound coils that regulate high-voltage current.

**Digi Power X** (DGXX), formerly a bitcoin miner called Digihost Technology, rebranded in March 2025 around a pivot to AI infrastructure. The company owns hydroelectric and thermal power assets in Alabama, New York, and North Carolina, with roughly 400 megawatts (MW) in its development pipeline. Because it already owns operating power plants with *substations* in place, it argues it can skip the *grid interconnection* queue that torments greenfield data center developers. “Traditional data center developers face 6 to 12 month wait times for transformer equipment and years for grid connection approvals,” the company has written in investor materials. “DGXX’s integrated power plants eliminate these bottlenecks.”

The tweet adds a layer the company’s public filings do not: that DGXX specifically acquired all necessary transformers from Siemens Energy (ENR.DE) — the Frankfurt-listed grid technology company that Siemens AG (SIE.DE) spun off in 2020 — and that this was highlighted in investor presentations as a time-to-market advantage. That specific claim does not appear in any SEC filing, press release, or shareholder letter reviewed as of May 2026. The documented advantage is structural: existing substations mean DGXX does not need to enter the large power transformer queue in the same way greenfield rivals do. Whether DGXX also secured discrete equipment orders from Siemens Energy is plausible but unverified in public sources — the claim may originate from a gated investor presentation or conference call not captured in EDGAR filings.

What is on the record is that the power-ownership strategy is producing signed contracts. In April 2026, DGXX announced a $19.6 million, 24-month *bare-metal GPU* rental agreement with SubQ AI — the company’s first AI revenue deal. Days later it signed a 10-year master services agreement with Cerebras Systems for a purpose-built 40 MW AI data center campus in Columbiana, Alabama, with an initial contract value of roughly $1.1 billion and total potential value of $2.5 billion including renewals. The on-site substation at Columbiana is already completed; grid interconnection with Alabama Power is finalized. The transformer advantage — structural or otherwise — is embedded in the asset before a single GPU rack is installed.

The company is not yet profitable. FY2025 revenue was $34.2 million against a net loss of $28.4 million (of which $22.2 million was non-cash charges). Cash stood at $78.5 million with zero long-term debt — a clean balance sheet for a company about to scale capital-intensively. In May 2026, DGXX upsized its *at-the-market* equity offering by $100 million, signaling it expects to need fresh capital to fund the Columbiana Phase 2 and the broader pipeline. Investors backing the thesis are ultimately betting that owning power infrastructure — rather than waiting to procure it — is the durable moat in an era when electrical lead times are measured in years, not quarters.

concepts.definition: A high-voltage transformer used to step electricity up or down for long-distance transmission. Building an AI data center typically requires at least one; lead times as of 2025 run from two to four years, making them a critical-path item for any new facility.

A specialized transformer that raises the output voltage of a power plant’s generator to the higher level needed for grid transmission. Demand for GSUs has risen 274% since 2019 as data centers increasingly seek on-site generation to bypass interconnection queues.

The formal process of connecting a new facility to the utility grid, including engineering studies, regulatory approvals, and physical equipment installation. For large loads this process can take several years, and it is a major constraint on new data center development.

GPU compute rented without any hypervisor or virtualization layer between the tenant and the hardware. Tenants get raw, dedicated hardware access — higher performance than shared cloud instances, but less flexibility and typically offered on longer-term contracts.

A mechanism that lets a public company sell newly issued shares gradually into the open market at prevailing prices, without the fixed-price structure of a traditional underwritten deal. It raises capital flexibly but dilutes existing shareholders over time.

An electrical facility containing transformers and switching gear that steps voltage up or down between a power source and end users. Owning a substation eliminates the need to queue for utility-owned infrastructure and is a key element of DGXX’s claimed supply chain advantage.

fact_check: The tweet’s central claim — that DGXX specifically acquired transformers from Siemens Energy and highlighted this in investor presentations as a time-to-market advantage — cannot be verified from any publicly available document, including SEC filings, press releases, and shareholder letters reviewed as of May 2026. The documented advantage is structural: DGXX’s existing power plants come with substations already built, so the company does not need to enter the large power transformer procurement queue in the way greenfield developers do. The Siemens sourcing claim may originate from a conference call or gated investor presentation not captured in public filings; it is plausible but unconfirmed.
